source: Liang et al. (2023/24) Can LLMs provide useful feedback on research papers? (GPT-4 vs human reviews)
finding: GPT-4 review comments overlap with human reviewer comments about as much as two humans overlap with each other.
numbers: Nature family: 30.85% GPT-4 vs one human, 28.58% human vs human; 57.55% of GPT-4 comments raised by at least one human. ICLR (1,709 papers): 39.23% vs 35.25%. Shuffled feedback: overlap fell to 0.43% (Nature) and 3.91% (ICLR).
limits: Overlap measured by a GPT-4 matching step (F1 82.4% for matching, 96.8% for extraction). Overlap is not correctness. Human reviewers themselves agree only about a third of the time.
agent_relevance: A model critic finds the same issues a human often finds, and the shuffle control shows the feedback is paper-specific. Fits G5 only if the critic is a screen, not a judge.

source: Liang et al. (2023/24) user study of GPT-4 feedback
finding: Researchers rated GPT-4 feedback on their own papers as useful, but it is shallow on method design.
numbers: 308 researchers from 110 US institutions. 57.4% found it helpful or very helpful. 82.4% found it more beneficial than feedback from at least some human reviewers.
limits: Self-selected volunteers who uploaded their own papers. GPT-4 tends to ask for more datasets and struggles with in-depth method critique.
agent_relevance: Useful as a cheap first-pass critic, weak where the agent most needs a check (the method).

source: Liang et al. (2023/24) overlap by paper quality
finding: GPT-4 overlaps more with human reviewers on weaker papers. It catches what many reviewers agree is wrong.
numbers: ICLR overlap: oral 30.63%, rejected 43.80% (47.09% in one breakdown). Comments raised by 3 or more reviewers overlap more with GPT-4 (31.67% Nature; 39.33% ICLR).
limits: Observational. Could also mean GPT-4 produces generic complaints that fit any weak paper.
agent_relevance: A critic catches consensus flaws, not rare ones. Do not expect it to find a novel error.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: automated reviewer
finding: An LLM reviewer with self-reflection, ensembling and a 1-shot example reaches near-human accuracy at predicting accept or reject.
numbers: 500 ICLR 2022 papers. Best: GPT-4o, 5 reflection rounds, 5 ensembled reviews, 1-shot: balanced accuracy 0.65 vs human 0.66; AUC 0.65 vs 0.65; F1 0.57 vs 0.49; FNR 0.39 vs 0.52; FPR 0.31 vs 0.17. Plain GPT-4o 0-shot: balanced accuracy 0.61. Raw Sonnet 3.5: 0.52 (accepts nearly everything, FPR 0.95).
limits: Human baseline is the NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment, not the same papers. Raw Sonnet 3.5 was uncalibrated. Reject-heavy dataset.
agent_relevance: Shows reflection plus ensembling in code lifts a model critic. Gain from 0.61 to 0.65 is small and needs the threshold set in code (G5).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: reviewer built into the loop
finding: The AI Scientist pipeline uses its own LLM reviewer to score papers it writes. The reviewer is an in-loop stand-in for peer review.
numbers: Reviewer uses GPT-4o with 5 reflections, 5 ensembled reviews, then an LLM meta-review acting as Area Chair.
limits: Generator and reviewer come from the same model family, so the self-preference risk in G5 applies.
agent_relevance: An existing example of peer review as an LLM-agent operator. Keep the reviewer blind to authorship and the proposed answer.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: Expert reviewers rated LLM ideas as more novel than human ideas. But reviewers disagree a lot, and an LLM judge is near chance.
numbers: 79 expert reviewers, 49 ideas per condition. Overall score: human 4.68, AI 4.85, AI+human rerank 5.34 (p=0.04). Reviewer agreement 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021: 66.0%; ICLR 2024 LLM papers: 71.9%). Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker accuracy 53.3%, below inter-reviewer agreement. Of 4,000 seed ideas only about 200 were non-duplicate.
limits: Ideas judged without running experiments. Novelty is subjective. Rater agreement is low, so the ground truth itself is noisy.
agent_relevance: Supports G8: model judging of ideas is near chance, and an execution step is needed. Idea pools also collapse to duplicates.

source: Si et al. (2024) LLM predicting accepted vs rejected ICLR proposals
finding: LLMs pick the accepted paper from a rejected one above chance, with no gain from few-shot or chain-of-thought.
numbers: Pairs of accepted vs rejected ICLR submissions: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4% zero-shot, GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%.
limits: Papers rewritten into a standard proposal format. Pairwise, not absolute.
agent_relevance: Extra prompting did not help here, consistent with the view that scaffolds must carry a check, not more words.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Are We There Yet? Risks of LLMs in peer review
finding: LLM reviewers can be manipulated by hidden text in the manuscript and give high scores to incomplete papers.
numbers: Simulation: manipulating 5% of reviews makes 12% of papers lose top-30% positions. LLM reviewers 4.5 times more consistent than humans with limitations that authors disclose. Ratings (LLM Review / AI Scientist / AgentReview): title only 4.35/2.96/4.83; title+abstract+intro 5.11/3.36/5.76; whole paper 5.34/3.41/5.82.
limits: Tested on specific review systems and ICLR-style data.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge rates a paper nearly the same with a fraction of its content. Reviews must be tied to executed evidence, not to text (G2, G3).

source: Ye et al. (2024) prestige and length bias
finding: LLM review systems prefer longer papers and well-known authors.
numbers: All three review systems show higher ratings with longer input. Attributing a paper to well-known researchers or institutions gives more favorable reviews in single-blind setting.
limits: Only direction recorded here; sizes are in the paper figures.
agent_relevance: Supports length-normalised scoring and authorship-blind critics (G5).

source: Liang et al. (2024) Monitoring AI-modified content in AI-conference peer reviews
finding: A measurable share of peer review text at AI conferences was substantially modified by an LLM after ChatGPT.
numbers: 6.5% (CoRL 2023) to 16.9% (EMNLP 2023) of text; ICLR 2024 10.6% of review sentences (from about 1.6% at the start of the window).
limits: Population-level estimate from a distribution model, not a per-review detector.
agent_relevance: Peer review itself is now partly model output, so a model critic and a model-written review share errors (G4).

source: Liang et al. (2024) who uses LLMs in reviews
finding: LLM-modified reviews cluster where reviewer effort is low and make reviews more alike.
numbers: Estimated LLM share is higher in reviews with lower confidence, submitted within 3 days of the deadline, and from reviewers who reply less to author rebuttals. Linked to homogenised review content.
limits: Correlational; the authors say they cannot make a causal claim.
agent_relevance: Correlated review errors: two model critics agree because of shared training, not independent checks (G4).

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench: computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: Agents with code and data supplied can often rerun easy reproductions, but fail on the hardest.
numbers: 270 tasks from 90 papers (CS, social science, medicine). CORE-Agent with GPT-4o: 60.00% Easy, 57.78% Medium, 21.48% Hard. GPT-4o-mini CORE-Agent: 44.44%, 32.59%, 16.30%.
limits: Task accuracy counts only fully correct answers. 2024 models; later work shows large gains.
agent_relevance: Reproduction (rerun) is a replication check an agent can do; the hard level needs installing and debugging, as in G2.

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench scaffold effect
finding: Task-specific hints in the scaffold raised accuracy more than a bigger budget did.
numbers: Task-specific modifications lifted Easy from 35.6% to 60.60% in one comparison. Raising the cost limit moved GPT-4o only from 26% to 31%.
limits: Hints were written after seeing agent failures on the dev set.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that fixes known failure modes beats more tokens. Matches G7.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: replicate ML research from scratch
finding: Agents replicate ML papers poorly; humans do better with time.
numbers: 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral papers, 8,316 gradable tasks. BasicAgent: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 21.0%, o1-high 13.2%, DeepSeek-R1 6.0%, Gemini 2.0 Flash 3.2%. Human ML PhDs on 3-paper subset: 41.4% after 48 hours vs o1 26.6%.
limits: 3 runs per paper. Models often stopped early claiming they were done. Rubric made with original authors.
agent_relevance: Agents declare success early. A code-controlled stopping rule matters (G6 and the counted-step principle).

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench scaffold sensitivity
finding: Changing only the agent prompt and forcing it to keep working changed scores a lot and in opposite directions by model.
numbers: IterativeAgent (cannot end early, piecemeal prompts): o1-high 24.4% (vs 13.2%), o3-mini-high 8.5%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 16.1% (down from 21.0%). o1 with 36-hour limit 26.0%. PaperBench Code-Dev (no execution) o1 43.4%.
limits: Effect depends on model; the authors say it shows sensitivity to prompting.
agent_relevance: A scaffold must be tested per model at equal budget (G7).

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench LLM judge
finding: An LLM grader against a rubric is a workable stand-in for a human grader, when tuned and scaffolded.
numbers: Best judge o3-mini-high with custom scaffolding: F1 0.83 on the auxiliary evaluation against human gold labels.
limits: Judge validated on a small gold set. Rubric written by humans.
agent_relevance: Rubric-based grading with human-made criteria is closer to G3 than free-form model opinion.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) SocSci-Repro-Bench
finding: Coding agents with code and data now reproduce most social science results.
numbers: 221 tasks, four disciplines. Claude Code task accuracy 93.4% (paper level 78.0%), Codex 62.1% (35.8%). Both 100% on 10 non-reproducible tasks. No-answer failures: Codex 17.8% of tasks, Claude Code 0%. Claude Code by language: Python 100%, Stata 94.4%, R 91.9%.
limits: Only 10 non-reproducible tasks. Reproduction is not replication on new data.
agent_relevance: Executing a check is within reach. The harder skill is saying it cannot be done.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) memorisation control
finding: Results are not mainly memory of the papers.
numbers: Accuracy before vs after training cutoff: Claude Code 93.3% vs 96.2%; Codex 62.9% vs 62.5%. Metadata recall: only 11.1% of papers fully identified.
limits: Cutoffs are model-specific and approximate.
agent_relevance: The agent performs the computation, not recall. Good for held-out checks.

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) paper PDF access
finding: Showing the original paper helps a little and hurts the ability to flag impossible reproductions.
numbers: Claude Code 93.4% to 94.5%; Codex 62.1% to 65.4%. Non-reproducible tasks: Claude Code 100% to 63.3%; Codex 100% to 90.0%.
limits: Small N for non-reproducible tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not show the checker the claimed answer (G5: no proposed answer).

source: Alizadeh et al. (2026) confirmatory prompt nudging
finding: Telling the agent to find defensible approaches that match the paper makes it fabricate output when reproduction is impossible.
numbers: Overall accuracy rose (Claude 93.4% to 94.1%; Codex 62.1% to 74.1%), but non-reproducible tasks fell: Claude 100% to 70.0%, Codex 90.0% to 60.0%. Codex failures fell 17.8% to 0.5%.
limits: Prompt written by the authors to be adversarial.
agent_relevance: Same mechanism as p-hacking: goal framing toward a known target. Never give the agent the target answer; require it to report divergence.

source: Kohler et al. (2026) Read the Paper, Write the Code
finding: Agents given only the methods text and data recover most published results, and many discrepancies trace to underspecified papers.
numbers: 48 papers, four scaffolds, four LLMs. Best system completed 92-100% of papers and 66-90% of cells; coefficient signs correct 75-91% (naive baseline 68%). Best agent reproduced coefficients within the original 95% CI over 80% of the time.
limits: Human audit confirmed 92% of flagged divergences but only 67% of error-source labels (LLM attribution).
agent_relevance: Independent re-implementation is a stronger replication than rerun. LLM error attribution is only 67% reliable, so verify with code.

source: Nguyen et al. (2026) ReplicatorBench
finding: Agents design and run replications well but fail at finding new data and at judging replicability.
numbers: 19 claims, replicable and non-replicable, three stages. Interpretation LLMEval: o3 94.54, GPT-5 91.26, GPT-5-mini 87.02, GPT-4o 82.25. Extraction: human 71.33 vs GPT-5 63.65. GPT-5-mini macro F1 47.86 on outcome classification.
limits: Small benchmark. Code translated to Python can alter numbers.
agent_relevance: Replication on new data is where agents stall; held-out data must be supplied by the program (G3).

source: Smaldino and McElreath (2016) The natural selection of bad science
finding: An evolutionary model shows incentives for publishing select for low rigor, and replication slows but does not stop this.
numbers: Meta-analysis of power: mean power 0.24, no increase over time (R2=0.00097). In the model without replication, power and false positive rate go to 1.
limits: Abstract model; parameters are assumed, not fitted to a field.
agent_relevance: Treat any selection-by-output loop as a pressure toward fitting. Replication must be rewarded explicitly (G3).

source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: A Bayesian argument that the chance a significant finding is true depends on power, bias and number of tests.
numbers: PPV = (1-b)R/(R-bR+a). Corollaries 1-6: smaller studies, smaller effects, more flexibility, more tested relationships, more interests, and hotter fields all lower the chance a finding is true.
limits: Theoretical; assumed priors. Later empirical work disputed the size of the claim.
agent_relevance: An agent trying many candidates against a few checks is the high-flexibility case: a pass becomes weak evidence (G3).

source: Liang et al. (2023/24) position bias of LLM feedback
finding: Matching probability falls down the comment list, so LLM feedback aligns with human feedback mostly in the first comments.
numbers: A human comment in the second quarter of the list had 16.74% chance of overlap in one analysis, decreasing from the first quarter.
limits: Position analysis depends on the matching pipeline.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on one pass of model critique; use code to force coverage of method sections.

source: Kohler et al. (2026) information isolation design
finding: The system hides code, results and paper from the reimplementing agent, then compares output to the original cell by cell in code.
numbers: Deterministic cell-level comparison; an LLM step assigns root causes; 49 of 53 flagged divergences confirmed (92%).
limits: Papers were 56.3% Stata, 27.1% R, none Python.
agent_relevance: A working template of replication as an operator: separate generator, hidden target, code comparator. Maps to G3 and G5.

source: Lu et al. (2024) vs Si et al. (2024) judge validity across tasks
finding: Reviewer-style LLM judges that look near-human on accept or reject do much worse at ranking ideas.
numbers: AI Scientist reviewer balanced accuracy 0.65 on ICLR 2022 papers; Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker 53.3% on idea pairs in Si et al.
limits: Different tasks, different data.
agent_relevance: Judge validity is task-specific. Calibrate every judge against held-out human labels before use.
